analysis.one_liner: Limits mandatory overtime for nurses at Medicare-participating hospitals, clinics, and home health agencies.
analysis.headline: Referred to two House committees in August 2026, the bill has received no committee action or vote, with the congressional session ending January 3, 2027.
analysis.plain_summary: Hospitals, ambulatory surgical centers, home health agencies, clinics, and other Medicare-participating providers could no longer force nurses to work beyond their scheduled shift, more than 48 hours a week, more than 12 consecutive hours, or without a 10-hour rest after a 12-hour shift [S2][S3]. The limits do not apply during declared emergencies, and a nurse could still volunteer for extra hours [S2][S3]. Nurses who refuse mandatory overtime or report violations would be protected from firing or retaliation, and providers could face civil fines of up to $10,000 per knowing violation [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Registered, licensed practical, and licensed vocational nurses at hospitals and other covered providers gain a legal limit on forced overtime, a guaranteed rest period after long shifts, and protection from retaliation for refusing or reporting violations [S2][S3]. Patients gain care from nurses who are not working fatigued; the bill's own findings cite research linking long nurse hours to medical errors [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Bars providers from requiring nurses to work beyond a scheduled shift, over 48 hours in a week, over 12 consecutive hours, or during the 10 hours after the 12th hour worked.
Protects nurses from being fired, demoted, disciplined, or reported to state licensing boards for refusing mandatory overtime or reporting violations, and gives them a complaint process with HHS.

Requires providers to post nurse schedules, document any emergency overtime in writing, and publicly post notices of nurses' rights, with civil money penalties up to $10,000 per knowing violation and higher penalties for repeat offenders.
The bill's findings cite studies that limits on nurse work hours improve occupational and patient safety, and note 18 states have already restricted mandatory overtime for nurses.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, home health agencies, clinics, and other Medicare providers bear the cost: they would need to fill staffing gaps with additional hires or voluntary shifts instead of mandatory overtime, document schedules, and face penalties for violations [S2][S3]. Facilities with chronic understaffing get no exemption, since the emergency exception explicitly excludes understaffing [S3].

drawbacks.text: Providers in areas with persistent nursing shortages would have to cover shifts through hiring or voluntary overtime; the emergency exception deliberately excludes chronic understaffing, so a hospital that cannot recruit would have no mandate escape valve.

Enforcement depends on nurses filing complaints with HHS and on investigations the Secretary must conduct, and the penalty for a first knowing violation is capped at $10,000, which some hospitals may treat as a cost of business.

The bill does not limit voluntary overtime, so nurses who take extra shifts by choice could still accumulate very long total hours, and it does not address the underlying pay and staffing problems that drive overtime in the first place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety case is well documented in the bill itself: research cited in its findings links fatigued nurses to medical errors, and 18 states have already imposed similar limits [S3]. The costs fall on hospitals that currently rely on forced overtime to cover gaps, and they are real, especially for rural and understaffed facilities, but the emergency carve-out preserves flexibility in true crises. A narrow limitation: the complaint-and-penalty enforcement structure is modest for a national mandate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in August 2026 and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or vote as the session runs down toward January 3, 2027.

narrative.text: Rep. Doris Matsui, a Democrat, and Rep. Jen Kiggans of Virginia, a Republican, jointly introduced the Nurse Overtime and Patient Safety Act on August 6, 2026.
The bill was referred to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction; no further action appears in the record.
Four additional House members cosponsored the bill: three Democrats and one Republican.

The bill attaches its overtime limits to Medicare participation, so any hospital, psychiatric hospital, critical access hospital, ambulatory surgical center, home health agency, rehabilitation agency, clinic, rural health clinic, or federally qualified health center that takes Medicare must comply.
The bill takes effect one year after enactment, so even if passed quickly it would not change practice until 2027 at the earliest.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: As of now, nothing has happened, which leaves hospitals free to continue requiring nurses to work beyond scheduled shifts and long consecutive hours; nurses and patients are no better off until the bill moves.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced jointly by a Democrat and a Republican, and its four additional cosponsors split 3 to 1 between the parties; no recorded opposition vote exists because no chamber has voted on it.

industries.note: Providers would lose the ability to require nurses to work past scheduled shifts, long consecutive hours, or without rest, and would face documentation requirements and fines up to $10,000 per knowing violation. Their interest in keeping forced overtime available runs against nurses' rest and patients' safety, per the research cited in the bill's findings.

industries.industry: Registered, licensed practical, and licensed vocational nurses
industries.note: Nurses gain enforceable limits on mandatory overtime, a 10-hour rest rule after 12-hour shifts, whistleblower and anti-retaliation protections, and posted schedules. Better-rested nurses directly serve patient safety.

industries.industry: Nurse staffing agencies and per-diem nursing
industries.note: With mandatory overtime off the table, hospitals needing to fill gaps would have to turn to voluntary shifts, agency staffing, or new hires, increasing demand for flexible staffing arrangements.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has five supporters in the House, two committee referrals, and no committee action, in a Congress that ends January 3, 2027. Late-introduced health bills that sit unmarked up in committee almost never reach the floor in the remaining months, so the realistic path is expiration at the end of this Congress, with supporters needing to reintroduce it in the next one.
